title: What to keep from Montaigne
hookLine: curiosity, doubt, gentleness, laughter at ourselves

cards: Moving day. The truck comes at nine, the boxes are full, and there's one small bag left for the things you won't let the movers touch. Not much fits, so you choose.
Montaigne's book is a big, rambling house of a book, with a room for nearly everything, and tomorrow this path closes the door on it. Today is the small bag.
Four things seem worth carrying out: curiosity, doubt, gentleness, and laughter at ourselves.

teach.b: First, curiosity. Montaigne wanted to know how other people lived. He loved travel for the new and the different, and he turned the same curiosity on himself: his moods, his habits, his own changing mind.
Nothing was too small to look at. Second, doubt.
He took a question as a kind of motto: what do I know? Not despair. A brake.
It kept him from being too sure, especially when being sure meant condemning someone. A man who doubts his own judgment is slower to burn a neighbor for a witch.
Third, gentleness. He hated cruelty, and said so, even cruelty to animals.
When he played with his cat, he wondered whether she was playing with him. A gentle mind leaves room for the other creature's point of view. Fourth, laughter at ourselves.

On the highest throne in the world, he says, we still sit on our own bottom. He didn't laugh at other people's faith or pain, only at the human habit of taking ourselves too seriously, starting with his own.
The four hold each other up. Curiosity without doubt turns into collecting opinions to win arguments. Doubt without gentleness turns cold.
Gentleness without laughter gets heavy. Laughter without curiosity is just mockery.

At the very end of his book, Montaigne asks not for a severe wisdom, but for a cheerful and sociable one. If only one thing fits in the bag, today's line picks curiosity, because it keeps the other three moving.

how: Readers who spend time with Montaigne often come away keeping one habit rather than a doctrine, such as asking 'what do I know?' before judging, or laughing at their own self-importance.

games.q: what does “what to keep from montaigne” mean?
o: the rules Montaigne set for a strict, serious life
four habits of Montaigne's worth carrying with you
the sayings painted on his library's ceiling beams

games.q: what to keep: tap the pairs.
p: nothing too small to look at
wondering if the cat plays with him
we still sit on our own bottom

s: Montaigne's doubt was a kind of despair
it worked more like a brake, keeping him from being too sure, especially when condemning someone.
he laughed mostly at other people's beliefs
he laughed at the human habit of taking ourselves too seriously, starting with himself.
at the end of his book he asks for a cheerful, sociable wisdom

games.q: you can carry only one of Montaigne's four habits out of his book. which one does today's line pick?
o: doubt, because it keeps you humble.
curiosity, because it keeps the others moving.
laughter, because it's the most fun.
games.why: the line for today is keep curious: curiosity keeps doubt, gentleness and laughter from going stale.

practice: Say the four quietly, curiosity, doubt, gentleness, laughter, and notice which one tugs at you, maybe because you have it, maybe because you don't.
Then let a real moment from this week come to mind, a hard conversation, a quick judgment, a bad mood, and hold that quality up to it like a lamp, just looking at what it would have changed.

wordCard.voice: What to keep from Montaigne. Curiosity, doubt, gentleness, and laughter at ourselves, four habits that hold each other up. Today's word.

orig.note: Montaigne's French (in Latin letters): what do I know? The question he took as a kind of motto.

carryVoice: Your line: keep curious. Montaigne aimed his curiosity at himself first. Rest well.
